God will come to defend and change his people. They will no longer be deaf, blind, or lame (see {{Isaiah 6:10|Isaiah 6:10}}). Instead, they will be pure, holy, and saved.

- *Lebanon … Carmel … Sharon*: There will be a reversal of earlier judgments (see {{Isaiah 2:13|Isaiah 2:13}}; {{Isaiah 10:34|10:34}}; {{Isaiah 29:17|29:17}}; {{Isaiah 33:9|33:9}}). 

- *glory … splendor of our God*: See also {{Isaiah 6:3|Isaiah 2:3}}; {{Isaiah 40:5|40:5}}.
*Limp hands* and *feeble knees *express discouragement and anxiety (see {{Hebrews 12:12|Hebrews 12:12}}).

- *do not fear!*: The Lord assures his people of his presence and purpose (see also {{Isaiah 7:4|Isaiah 7:4}}; {{Isaiah 10:24|10:24}}; {{Isaiah 40:9|40:9}}; {{Isaiah 43:1|43:1}}; {{Isaiah 44:2|44:2}}; {{Isaiah 54:4|54:4}}). 

- The main message of the good news is that God is coming to save his people (see also {{Isaiah 40:9|Isaiah 40:9}}; {{Isaiah 52:7|52:7}}; {{Isaiah 62:11|62:11}}). God's arrival brings spiritual change and rescue from enemies.

*eyes … ears*: There will be a transformation from spiritual blindness and deafness to understanding and knowing God ({{Isaiah 6:10|Isaiah 6:10}}; {{Isaiah 29:18|29:18}}; {{Isaiah 32:3|32:3}}; {{Isaiah 42:7|42:7}}; see also {{Luke 7:22|Luke 7:22}}; {{Acts 26:18|Acts 26:18}}).

*the lame … and the mute*: This promise shows that God will remove all disabilities. He will bring healing and wholeness (see {{Matthew 11:5|Matthew 11:5}}; {{Matthew 12:22|12:22}}; {{Mark 7:37|Mark 7:37}}; {{Acts 3:7-8|Acts 3:7–8}}).

- The image of the highway recalls Israel’s crossing through the Red Sea ({{Isaiah 51:10|Isaiah 51:10}}). 

- *only those who walk*: This means that only those who follow God will walk on his holy path. God's goal in salvation is for humans to share his character and act like him (see {{Ephesians 5:1-2|Ephesians 5:1–2}}; {{1 Peter 2:21|1 Peter 2:21}}).

*Zion*: The prophecy goes beyond Israel's return from exile to the final establishment of God's kingdom on earth. This kingdom will be full of joy and happiness, with no sorrow or mourning (see also {{Isaiah 25:7|Isaiah 25:7}}; {{Isaiah 51:11|51:11}}; {{Revelation 21:4|Revelation 21:4}}).

King Sennacherib of Assyria ruled from 705 to 681 BC. Hezekiah, like many other kings under Assyrian control, declared his independence when Sennacherib became king during a difficult time. By 701 BC, Sennacherib was ready to punish Hezekiah. Sennacherib claimed he conquered 46 fortified cities and many villages, taking 200,146 captives. Hezekiah tried to appease Sennacherib (see {{2 Kings 18:14-16|2 Kings 18:14–16}}), but it was too late.

Jerusalem’s rescue from King Sennacherib of Assyria is a main event in {{Isaiah 1:1-39:8|Isaiah 1–39}}. The Lord promised to save his people. He would remain present with Jerusalem (see{{Isaiah 7:14|7:14}}). He would also keep a remnant, a small group who would survive (see study note on Isaiah 10:20). 

Much of the land became empty and the population greatly reduced. This happened because Judah made a foolish alliance with Assyria (chapters{{Isaiah 7:1-8:22|7–8}}). Even so, the Lord did not allow total defeat. He preserved his people through Hezekiah, a faithful king.

Hezekiah faced the same kind of test that King Ahaz had faced. It was a test of trust in the Lord. In chapter{{Isaiah 36:1-22|36}}, the Assyrian officer repeats the word *trust* as he challenges the people. But Hezekiah had learned from the earlier warnings in chapters{{Isaiah 13:1-35:10|13–35}}. At least at first, he trusted God and passed the test.

This story also appears in {{2 Kings 18:13-20:19|2 Kings 18:13–20:19}}.

- Lachish was a city overlooking the hills west of Jerusalem. It needed to be captured before attacking Jerusalem. 

- The aqueduct that supplies water to the upper pool was on the north side of Jerusalem, not the Gihon Spring in the Kidron Valley.

- Isaiah met Ahaz on this road leading to the field where cloth is washed about 33 years earlier (see {{Isaiah 7:3|Isaiah 7:3}}). At that time, he urged Ahaz to trust God. However, Ahaz trusted Assyria instead, leading to this desperate situation. Now, the challenge to trust God came from mocking foreign voices (see {{Isaiah 28:11-13|Isaiah 28:11–13}}).
Eliakim eventually advanced in rank, while Shebna was demoted (see {{Isaiah 22:15-24|Isaiah 22:15–24}}).
The title *great king* is similar to the title *emperor*.

The Assyrian chief of staff tried to use intimidation to negotiate a peaceful settlement. In his first speech ({{Isaiah 36:4-10|Isaiah 36:4–10}}), he correctly argued that Egypt could not rescue them but incorrectly accused Hezekiah of misplaced trust in the Lord. 

Interestingly, the Assyrian did not view the contest as between the gods of Assyria and the Lord, but rather between Sennacherib (the great king) and the Lord.
*In whom are you now trusting*: Judah had asked Egypt to help them (see {{Isaiah 30:1-5|Isaiah 30:1–5}}).

- *Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him*: Isaiah argued the same case, pointing to the Lord as the only reliable source of help ({{Isaiah 31:1-3|Isaiah 31:1–3}}, {{Isaiah 31:7|7}}; {{Isaiah 39:7|39:7}}). 

- A kind of reed that breaks easily grows near the Nile (see {{Ezekiel 29:6-7|Ezekiel 29:6–7}}).

- *We trust in the LORD our God*: Ironically, the Assyrian chief of staff knew about Isaiah's message and used it to his advantage ({{Isaiah 26:4|Isaiah 26:4}}; {{Isaiah 36:15|36:15}}; {{Isaiah 37:10|37:10}}). 

- Hezekiah showed his dedication to the Lord by tearing down the pagan shrines and altars ({{2 Kings 18:4|2 Kings 18:4}}). However, the Assyrians mistakenly thought Hezekiah had angered God by doing this.
At this time, cavalry mounted on horses was the newest military technology. The Assyrian chief of staff was mocking the Judeans because he knew that Judah had no trained men who knew how to ride.

*The LORD Himself said to me*: It was common for a king to claim that a god approved of their actions when they destroyed other kingdoms. This matched Isaiah’s prophecy in {{Isaiah 10:5-6|Isaiah 10:5–6}}.
Aramaic was the common language of the Assyrian Empire. The elite understood it, but the common people of Judah did not.

In the Assyrian chief of staff’s second speech, he claimed that his nation’s gods were more powerful than the God of Judah (compare {{Isaiah 10:9-10|Isaiah 10:9–10}}). The ability of God to rescue his people was in question. In the following events, the Lord surprised the Assyrian with his power ({{Isaiah 37:36-37|Isaiah 37:36–37}}).
*Do not let Hezekiah deceive you*: This public accusation against Hezekiah aimed to weaken the people's trust in him.
Hezekiah showed strong faith in the Lord, unlike Ahaz ({{Isaiah 7:1-25|Isaiah 7}}). Hezekiah’s faith led to rescue, while Ahaz’s lack of faith led to trouble (see {{Isaiah 7:9|Isaiah 7:9}}).

The Assyrian tried to lure the people of Jerusalem with supplies that the Lord promised to give to his obedient followers (see {{Isaiah 1:19|Isaiah 1:19}}; {{Isaiah 37:30-35|37:30–35}}; {{Deuteronomy 8:7-9|Deuteronomy 8:7–9}}). It was a tempting offer, but it was fake. It hid the truth of the exile that would have come after ({{Isaiah 36:17|Isaiah 36:17}}).

The people of Hamath and Arpad were moved to Samaria, where they worshipped the gods of Sepharvaim ({{2 Kings 17:24|2 Kings 17:24}}). This argument made sense to an Assyrian. If the Assyrian gods defeated the gods of other nations and the God of the Israelites in Samaria, would they not also defeat the God of Judah?

- Hezekiah responded to the threats by seeking the Lord’s favor.

- The king tore his clothes and wore sackcloth as a sign of mourning and prayer.

*Perhaps … God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh … defy the living God*: Hezekiah's hope was not based on Judah's or his own goodness, nor on the presence of the temple in Jerusalem. Instead, it was based on God responding to Assyria's disrespect.
God answered that he would deal with the Assyrians and rescue the remnant of his people from their distress (see {{Isaiah 63:9|Isaiah 63:9}}).
Libnah was a city on the Philistine plain near Lachish. Sennacherib was preparing to fight both Egypt and Jerusalem when he sent word to Hezekiah.
King Tirhakah of Ethiopia was then the ruler of Egypt.

- The argument was that Judah's god, like the gods of other nations already conquered by Assyria, would not be able to save Judah (see also {{Isaiah 36:18-20|Isaiah 36:18–20}}). 

- Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, Eden, and Telassar were cities in Mesopotamia.

When Hezekiah received Sennacherib’s boastful threat, he went back to the temple and prayed for help. His prayer was different from Ahaz’s reaction to danger decades earlier (see {{Isaiah 7:1-25|Isaiah 7}}).

- *God of Israel*: Hezekiah did not believe Sennacherib's false claims that the Lord was powerless. In his prayer, Hezekiah recognized that the Lord, as the creator, is the God of all the earth's kingdoms. The Lord rules over all kingdoms. 

- The mighty cherubim were in the temple on top of the ark of the covenant, which was God's throne in his temple (see study note on Leviticus 16:2; see also {{Psalm 80:1|Psalms 80:1}}; {{Psalm 99:1|99:1}}).

*You alone, O LORD, are God*: Hezekiah cared about the Lord's reputation, which Sennacherib had insulted. Hezekiah understood that if the Lord defeated the Assyrians and their gods, His holy name would be honored worldwide (see {{Exodus 9:16|Exodus 9:16}}; {{Exodus 14:4|14:4}}, {{Exodus 14:17-18|17–18}}; {{Joshua 2:9-11|Joshua 2:9–11}}; {{1 Samuel 4:7-8|1 Samuel 4:7–8}}).

*Because you have prayed*: Prayer has great power. God heard Hezekiah’s prayer and responded.

The Lord answered him with a message of hope.
*The Virgin Daughter of Zion*: Jerusalem is described as a young woman who taunts the Assyrian king (see also {{Isaiah 3:26|Isaiah 3:26}}).
*Against whom*: Sennacherib’s speech was not so much an insult against Judah as it was against the Lord.

Isaiah seems to be familiar with the typical royal Assyrian boasts, including that they possessed the highest mountains. These words sound very much like those found in the annals of the Assyrian kings inscribed on the walls of their temples.

*I have dug wells … I have dried up all the streams of Egypt*: Sennacherib's boasts show his attitude of independence. However, the Lord alone is sovereign over nature ({{Isaiah 42:15|Isaiah 42:15}}; {{Isaiah 43:19|43:19}}; {{Isaiah 44:27|44:27}}).

*I planned … that you should crush … into piles of rubble*: Assyria was God's agent of destruction, but the Assyrians did not understand they were just a tool in God's hand (see {{Isaiah 10:1-34|Isaiah 10}}), carrying out what God had planned long ago ({{Isaiah 14:24-27|Isaiah 14:24–27}}).
*your raging against Me*: Assyria was completely hostile to the Lord, which led to even greater condemnation for them.
*My hook … My bit*: The Assyrians would be taken away like animals, just as they had done to many of their captives.

*This year … the second year … the third year*: Due to the Assyrian siege and its impact on farming, the people of Judah could not plant and harvest as usual. The promise that life would return to normal after the siege reassured them that God was with them and would provide for their daily needs. They needed to build their trust in God over three years, believing that God's word would come true (see {{Isaiah 30:15|Isaiah 30:15}}, {{Isaiah 30:18|18}}). 

The idea was that after escaping the Assyrians, it would be too late to plant in the current year. They would have to wait until the fall of the second year to plant again and would harvest their first crop in the spring and summer of the third year.

In this prophecy of salvation, Isaiah assured Hezekiah that Jerusalem would be spared and that the remnant was under God’s protection. 

The names of Isaiah and his sons anticipated God's rescue (see {{Isaiah 7:1-11:16|Isaiah 7:1–11:16}}). The book’s record of God’s presence and rescue provided assurance that the Lord would always have a remnant that he will protect and rescue.
The passionate commitment of God includes his energetic zeal to keep his promise, the best guarantee his people could ever have (see also {{Isaiah 9:7|Isaiah 9:7}}).
*He will not enter … arrow … shield … siege ramp*: Despite their advanced military technology and great power, the Assyrians did not succeed against Jerusalem.
*for the sake of My servant David*: God had made a promise to David. He said that David’s royal family would continue forever (see {{Isaiah 9:6-7|Isaiah 9:6–7}}; {{2 Samuel 7:8-17|2 Samuel 7:8–17}}).

- The angel of the Lord was a special heavenly messenger through whom God acted on earth. Often, he delivered important messages (see {{Genesis 16:7-14|Genesis 16:7–14}}), but sometimes he brought judgment (see {{2 Samuel 24:16|2 Samuel 24:16}}). 

- *struck down 185,000 men*: The Lord began to fulfill his repeated promises: rescue of Jerusalem and judgment of Assyria (see {{Isaiah 10:16|Isaiah 10:16}}, {{Isaiah 10:33-34|33–34}}; {{Isaiah 30:31|30:31}}; {{Isaiah 31:8|31:8}}).

- *One day*: Sennacherib was likely killed in 681 BC, about twenty years after he left Jerusalem. 

- Esarhaddon ruled Assyria from 680 to 669 BC. It is ironic that Sennacherib, who mocked the Lord, was killed by his sons in the temple of his own god.

I*n those days*: This is a very general time statement. Hezekiah’s illness and healing likely happened before Jerusalem’s rescue ({{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}), even though Isaiah mentions it afterward. Merodach-baladan’s rule in Babylon ({{Isaiah 39:1|Isaiah 39:1}}) ended before Sennacherib’s invasion in 701 BC. The text order suggests a link between these events (see {{Isaiah 38:6|Isaiah 38:6}}).

The story of Hezekiah’s healing connects two events. It links the extension of Hezekiah’s life with Jerusalem’s rescue from the Assyrians.

These events happened before Jerusalem was saved. However, the book places them in this order because of their theme, not their time sequence. One main theme is the power of prayer (see {{Isaiah 37:14-20|Isaiah 37:14–20}}; {{Isaiah 38:2-3|38:2–3}}). The Lord truly listens.

Hezekiah learned to trust God. His father, Ahaz, had refused to trust the Lord. Because Hezekiah trusted God, Judah and Jerusalem were spared complete destruction by the Assyrians.

Still, Hezekiah was not the promised Messiah, the Son of David ({{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}; {{Isaiah 9:1-7|9:1–7}}; {{Isaiah 11:1-16|11:1–16}}; {{Isaiah 16:5|16:5}}; {{Isaiah 32:1|32:1}};{{Isaiah 33:17-22|33:17–22}}). He was a faithful king, but he was also human and would die. His failures and his sickness (chapters{{Isaiah 38:1-39:8|38–39}}) prepare the reader for the coming of the true Messiah described in chapters{{Isaiah 40:1-66:24|40–66}}.

*I have walked before You faithfully*: Hezekiah’s heart (his inner attitude and will) was right with the Lord for most of his reign ({{2 Kings 18:1-5|2 Kings 18:1–5}}). However, Hezekiah showed weakness when he relied on Egypt and did not act faithfully ({{Isaiah 31:1-9|Isaiah 31:1–9}}).
*the God of your father David*: Hezekiah followed David's example with faithfulness (see {{Isaiah 37:35|Isaiah 37:35}}; {{Isaiah 38:1-22|38:1–22}}).

*I will deliver you … I will defend this city*: This promise refers to saving Jerusalem ({{Isaiah 36:1-37:38|Isaiah 36–37}}). It also helps us understand Hezekiah’s illness and recovery. Just as Hezekiah gained 15 more years, Jerusalem also received a temporary relief (see {{Isaiah 39:1-8|Isaiah 39}}).
Hezekiah’s poem includes both lament ({{Isaiah 38:9-14|Isaiah 38:9–14}}) and praise ({{Isaiah 38:15-20|38:15–20}}). The praise remains restrained until the final verse.

*go through the gates of Sheol*: This image comes from an ancient belief that people enter death through gates (see {{Isaiah 14:9|Isaiah 14:9}}). Old Testament believers did not understand the afterlife as the New Testament describes it. They saw it as a shadowy place where all the dead gathered, and where no one praised God (see {{Isaiah 38:18|Isaiah 38:18}}; {{Psalm 88:10|Psalms 88:10}}; {{Psalm 115:17|115:17}}).
Hezekiah was very sad when he thought he might die. He believed that death would separate him from fellowship with God. He also feared losing time with his family and friends.
These images show how short human life is (compare {{2 Corinthians 5:1|2 Corinthians 5:1}}). They remind us that life on earth does not last long.
*I will walk slowly*: Hezekiah might have once taken his life and health for granted. Now he understood that God could take these gifts away at any time.
God’s restoration of Hezekiah’s health also symbolized the restoration from exile that Judah would experience in the future.

Hezekiah received a sign from the Lord. This sign reminds us of another sign that the prophet had offered to Ahaz ({{Isaiah 7:11|Isaiah 7:11}}). 

Ahaz and Hezekiah stand at the two ends of a long story in Judah’s history. Ahaz represents the ungodly king. Hezekiah represents the godly king. 

Ahaz brought disaster on his people through his choices. Hezekiah, in contrast, brought deliverance to his people. However, {{Isaiah 39:1-8|Isaiah 39}} shows that even Hezekiah’s story includes warning and future trouble.
Hezekiah could not visit the temple with an infection (see {{Leviticus 13:1-59|Leviticus 13}}). So, going to the temple means he is healthy again.

Merodach-baladan, the king of Babylon from 722 to 710 and 704 to 703 BC, planned to rebel against Assyria. He sought help from Hezekiah. His envoys visited after Hezekiah recovered from a serious illness but before Sennacherib's final attack in 701 BC.
Hezekiah was an example of godliness, prayer, and care for the people of Jerusalem. However, he disappointed the Lord by showing off his wealth and military power to the envoys from Babylon.
*silver … precious oils … his entire armory*: By showing these treasures, Hezekiah demonstrated to Babylon's envoys that he had the resources to be a valuable ally.

*carried off to Babylon*: This prophecy came before the prophecy about saving Jerusalem ({{Isaiah 37:35|Isaiah 37:35}}). Although this judgment and exile seem like a surprising end to Hezekiah's story, the exile of Israel and Judah was always a possibility ({{Isaiah 10:3-4|Isaiah 10:3–4}}, {{Isaiah 10:20-23|20–23}}). 

The Lord promised to protect Judah and Jerusalem from the Assyrians in 701 BC, but he warned Isaiah that worse would happen if they did not change. God showed his power and reliability by defeating the Assyrians, but the people did not change. The promises of {{Isaiah 2:1-5|Isaiah 2:1–5}} and {{Isaiah 4:2-6|4:2–6}} would only come true through judgment ({{Isaiah 4:4|4:4}}). 

Until the exile cleansed the nation's wrongdoings ({{Isaiah 6:5-7|Isaiah 6:5–7}}), their mission to other nations would not succeed.

This chapter introduces chapters{{Isaiah 40:1-66:24|40–66}}. In this section, comfort means the result of God's merciful actions toward people in the future. It includes encouragement, strength, and acceptance. 

God wants to rescue his people ({{Isaiah 40:1-11|Isaiah 40:1–11}}) and is fully capable of doing so ({{Isaiah 40:12-26|40:12–26}}). The exiles needed to trust God's promises and wait for their rescue ({{Isaiah 40:27-31|Isaiah 40:27–31}}; see also {{Isaiah 30:15-18|30:15–18}}).

At the end of chapter 39 Isaiah made an announcement about Babylon. The Babylonian government would take control of the southern kingdom. The Babylonian armies would force many people from the southern kingdom to leave their land. They would be forced to live in exile in Babylon.

Chapters 40 to 48 record messages of comfort to those people living in exile in Babylon. These messages were recorded as poems, prophecies and songs of praise. They were also recorded as arguments between God and others in a courtroom.

These messages make three things very clear. They make clear who God is, what false gods are and who God’s people were. First, God is the one true God who created everything and has always existed. No one and nothing is equal to God. Second, false gods are objects made by people and they have no power at all. False gods can’t tell people what’s going to happen or save people from their troubles. Third, the people of Jacob’s family line were God’s servants. God chose them to be witnesses to others that he is God.

God’s love for Jacob’s family line was strong and tender. God described himself as a shepherd who carried his people like lambs close to his heart. But his people complained that God had treated them badly. They thought that the exile showed that God didn’t care about them. God explained that they had gone into exile because of their sins. But he announced a new thing that he would do. He would bring his people back to Judah from Babylon. He would use the king of Persia as his tool to make this happen. That king would be named Cyrus.

God talked about someone called God’s servant in chapter 42. In many ways this servant is what the people of Israel were to be. By obeying God’s laws, they were to live in ways that were holy and just. They were to teach other nations about God and how to worship and honour him. In this way they would be a light for the Gentiles. New Testament writers showed how Jesus served God in these ways as well (Matthew 12:15–21). They understood that the poem about this servant was a prophecy about Jesus.

This section shares the good news of God's coming salvation. The Lord will support his people and judge His enemies. Salvation will occur through the arrival, suffering, and exaltation of the Lord's servant, the Messiah, Jesus Christ.

The rest of Isaiah offers a message of comfort and reveals God's character and his plans for Israel. As {{Isaiah 39:6-7|Isaiah 39:6–7}} predicted, Judah would face judgment and exile after Isaiah's time. Throughout {{Isaiah 40:1-66:24|Isaiah 40–66}}, Isaiah prophesied as if the exile in Babylon had already occurred. Thus, the Babylonian exile is the context for understanding these chapters.

- *Speak tenderly*: The prophet's message was to encourage Jerusalem with the good news of God's forgiveness, reconciliation, and restoration. 

- From the prophetic perspective, Israel’s sad days are gone because the exile has ended. 

- *she has received from the hand of the LORD double for all her sins*: Israel faced the full force of God's wrath ({{Isaiah 51:19-23|Isaiah 51:19–23}}; compare {{Isaiah 61:7|61:7}}).

- *A voice of one calling*: In {{Malachi 3:1|Malachi 3:1}}, this person (possibly the Elijah of {{Malachi 4:5|Malachi 4:5}}) was God's messenger who prepared the way for God's coming. In the Gospels, people identified this announcer as John the Baptist ({{Matthew 3:3|Matthew 3:3}}; {{Mark 1:3|Mark 1:3}}; {{Luke 3:4|Luke 3:4}}; {{John 1:23|John 1:23}}). 

- *Prepare the way … make a straight highway*: The announcer's message would speed up God's coming (see {{Isaiah 35:8|Isaiah 35:8}}). As God made a way for Israel through the Red Sea ({{Isaiah 43:16|Isaiah 43:16}}), a way would also be opened for the Lord (see {{Isaiah 52:11-12|52:11–12}}).

There is now a shift from announcing the good news to expecting God's arrival. The good news ({{Isaiah 40:1-2|Isaiah 40:1–2}}) is based on God himself. 

Isaiah described the Lord as coming on a highway through the desert (see {{Isaiah 35:1-10|Isaiah 35}}). However, the imagery is reversed here: In {{Isaiah 35:1-10|Isaiah 35}}, the people traveled to Zion, toward the Lord. Here, the Lord is coming toward his people (see also {{Isaiah 52:8|Isaiah 52:8}}, where both images are combined).

- The future display of God's glory would include Judah's return from exile but extend beyond that. The New Testament confirms that God's glory was revealed in Jesus Christ ({{John 1:14|John 1:14}}; {{Hebrews 1:3|Hebrews 1:3}}). 

- *the mouth of the LORD has spoken*: The promised salvation and judgment will surely happen because the Lord, who keeps his promises, has declared it (see {{Isaiah 1:20|Isaiah 1:20}}; {{Isaiah 58:14|58:14}}).

- *Cry out*: So that everyone can hear. 

- People are not worthy of the revelation of God’s glory because they are mortal.
All humans are mortal and temporary. In contrast, God continues with his plans and succeeds. Time does not stop him from doing what he wants (see {{Isaiah 14:24|Isaiah 14:24}}).
The *breath of the LORD* refers to God's spoken words of judgment (see {{Isaiah 4:4|Isaiah 4:4}}).

*the word of our God stands forever*: All of God’s words, including his plans and the written word, will succeed. God might change human expectations, but everything will follow his wise plan (see {{Isaiah 14:24|Isaiah 14:24}}; {{Isaiah 55:8-11|55:8–11}}; see also {{Matthew 25:34|Matthew 25:34}}).
God is coming to save and restore human beings (see also {{Isaiah 35:4|Isaiah 35:4}}; {{Revelation 22:12|Revelation 22:12}}).
God is the good news. He comes as a warrior to rescue his people with power, yet he also holds them gently like a shepherd.

- The Lord's rule is different from that of unjust and weak rulers, whom he will judge. His rule is compassionate, just, righteous, and powerful. 

- *His arm establishes His rule*: God showed his power in events such as: 

- the defeat of the Egyptians ({{Isaiah 63:12|Isaiah 63:12}}),

- the judgment of his enemies ({{Isaiah 30:30|Isaiah 30:30}}; {{Isaiah 48:14|48:14}}; {{Isaiah 51:9|51:9}}), and

- the rescue of his people ({{Isaiah 59:16|Isaiah 59:16}}).

Isaiah used the well-known biblical image of a shepherd to describe God's care for his people (see also {{Isaiah 49:10|Isaiah 49:10}}; {{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}; {{Jeremiah 3:15|Jeremiah 3:15}}; {{Jeremiah 23:4|23:4}}; {{Ezekiel 34:11-17|Ezekiel 34:11–17}}; {{Matthew 2:6|Matthew 2:6}}; {{John 10:1-18|John 10:1–18}}).

These rhetorical questions suggest the answer, “No one!” God alone created everything. He will judge creation ({{Isaiah 24:17|Isaiah 24:17}}), and only he can and will restore it through his salvation.
In response to Israel's questions (spoken by the prophet), the Lord declared that he is the unmatched God, a wise and sovereign creator who governs the nations.
God rules over all nations and their power structures. Compared to God, they are almost nothing. This includes the Babylonian Empire, which was just a tool in God's hand.
People valued Lebanon for its plentiful wood and wildlife (see {{Isaiah 2:13-16|Isaiah 2:13–16}}; {{Psalm 104:16-17|Psalm 104:16–17}}).

The nations, including their leaders ({{Isaiah 40:23|Isaiah 40:23}}), pagan structures ({{Isaiah 41:24|41:24}}, {{Isaiah 41:29|29}}; {{Isaiah 44:9-11|44:9–11}}), and all enemies of God's people ({{Isaiah 41:11-12|41:11–12}}), are worth nothing apart from God.

- *To whom … what image*: Earlier in the book, Isaiah showed that idolatry is foolish and empty ({{Isaiah 16:12|Isaiah 16:12}}; {{Isaiah 37:16-19|37:16–19}}). {{Isaiah 40:1-48:22|Isaiah 40–48}}, he gives a much longer argument against it.

An idol is an object that people make to represent a god or a religious idea. But these objects are made by human hands. Those who worship them do not see that they are only things people have made.

Idols have no power ({{Isaiah 41:7|Isaiah 41:7}}, {{Isaiah 41:22-24|22–24}}; {{Isaiah 48:14|48:14}}). They give people a false feeling of safety ({{Isaiah 42:17|Isaiah 42:17}}). They mislead people and cause deep disappointment ({{Isaiah 44:20|Isaiah 44:20}}; {{Isaiah 42:17|42:17}}; {{Isaiah 45:16|45:16}}, {{Isaiah 45:20|20}}). They cannot save or protect anyone.

In fact, idols are so weak that they can fall over ({{Isaiah 40:20|Isaiah 40:20}}; {{Isaiah 41:7|41:7}}). They compete with God’s glory ({{Isaiah 42:8|Isaiah 42:8}}). They also lower human dignity, because people bow down to things they have made ({{Isaiah 44:9|44:9}}; see also {{Isaiah 41:21-29|41:21–29}}). 

- The Lord, the true God, is not like idols. No one can compare to him (see {{Isaiah 40:25|Isaiah 40:25}}; {{Isaiah 46:5|46:5}}; {{Psalm 86:8|Psalms 86:8}}; {{Psalm 89:6|89:6}}). He is completely unique and without equal.

*an idol that will not topple*: This is a sarcastic remark. It would be embarrassing if the idol could not even stand (see {{Isaiah 40:18|Isaiah 40:18}}; {{Isaiah 41:7|41:7}}; {{1 Samuel 5:4|1 Samuel 5:4}}).

Idol worshipers do not recognize God or respond wisely to him. The faithful in Israel understand and see God's role in the story of redemption, which includes both exile and restoration ({{Isaiah 41:20|Isaiah 41:20}}).

- God rules as king over the entire earth (see {{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}; {{Psalm 2:4|Psalms 2:4}}; {{Psalm 80:1|80:1}}; {{Psalm 99:1|99:1}}; {{Psalm 102:12|102:12}}; {{Psalm 113:5|113:5}}). God is so vast and powerful that humans seem like grasshoppers in comparison. 

- Believing in God as the creator of the heavens and earth opposes the common Babylonian and Egyptian belief that the sun, moon, and stars are gods. 

- *like a curtain...a tent*: See also {{Psalm 104:2|Psalm 104:2}}.
*princes*: God is not impressed by human power or fame. Human strength and reputation do not change who God is.

*The Holy One* is a shorter form of *the Holy One of Israel*. This is a common name for God in the book of Isaiah (see also {{Isaiah 10:17|Isaiah 10:17}}; {{Isaiah 43:15|43:15}}; {{Psalm 22:3|Psalm 22:3}}).

*Lift up your eyes on high*: Just as God told Abraham to look into the sky ({{Genesis 15:5|Genesis 15:5}}), he also told Israel to look to the stars for encouragement (see also {{Isaiah 51:2-3|Isaiah 51:2–3}}). The cosmos shows God's great power and unmatched strength. The Strong One can strengthen the weak ({{Isaiah 40:27-31|Isaiah 40:27–31}}; see {{Psalm 147:5|Psalm 147:5}}).

*My way is hidden … ignored by my God*: The coming exile, a time when God's powerful presence and rescue would not be visible, would prompt questions (see also {{Isaiah 49:14|Isaiah 49:14}}; {{Isaiah 54:7|54:7}}; {{Lamentations 5:20-22|Lamentations 5:20–22}}).

- *know … understood*: Compare {{Isaiah 40:21|Isaiah 40:21}}. 

- *the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth*: Creation shows God's power and wisdom. He is also the Creator of the future world, a place of righteousness, justice, and peace ({{Isaiah 45:8|Isaiah 45:8}}; {{Isaiah 48:6-7|48:6–7}}; {{Isaiah 65:17-18|65:17–18}}). 

- *He will not grow tired or weary*: God does not have human limitations.

In this context, the weak are those who face persecution or oppression, like during the exile in Babylon. The Lord is their only help (see {{Isaiah 49:4-5|Isaiah 49:4–5}}; {{Isaiah 50:4|50:4}}; {{Psalm 68:9|Psalms 68:9}}; {{Psalm 119:28|119:28}}).

- *wait upon the LORD*: See {{Isaiah 33:2|Isaiah 33:2}}; {{Isaiah 49:23|49:23}}; {{Isaiah 51:5|51:5}}.

- *like eagles*: This strong image of rescue reminded readers of the exodus event from long ago ({{Exodus 19:4|Exodus 19:4}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:10-12|Deuteronomy 32:10–12}}; see also {{Psalm 103:5|Psalm 103:5}}).

- The nations gathering for a trial must listen quietly to God's arguments. 

- *Let them come forward and testify*: Literally *let them find new strength,* which is a reference to {{Isaiah 40:31|Isaiah 40:31}}. 

- God invited the nations to come and speak, challenging them to counter his case.

The Lord invited the nations to a trial to show that he alone is God. They could not defend themselves as he announced that a king from the east ({{Isaiah 41:2|Isaiah 41:2}}) would defeat Babylon, allowing Israel to return.

- The king from the east was Cyrus, the Persian king who conquered Babylon in 539 BC. He allowed the Jews to return to their land and rebuild Jerusalem in 538 BC ({{Ezra 1:1-4|Ezra 1:1–4}}). 

Isaiah’s prophecies about Cyrus ({{Isaiah 44:28-45:13|Isaiah 44:28–45:13}}; {{Isaiah 48:14-15|48:14–15}}) encouraged Israel to see the Lord as the ruler over all human history, including the actions of great kings. 

- *He hands nations over to him*: As victorious as the conquering Cyrus was, he was still subject to the Lord.

- *the generations from the beginning?*: God rules over everything. From the very beginning, he has guided each stage of history according to his plan.

- In the book of Revelation, Jesus calls himself *the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End* ({{Revelation 1:8|Revelation 1:8}}, {{Revelation 1:17|17}}; {{Revelation 2:8|2:8}}; {{Revelation 21:6|21:6}}; {{Revelation 22:13|22:13}}). 

- *I am He*: The Lord alone is God (see also {{Isaiah 43:10|Isaiah 43:10}}, {{Isaiah 43:13|13}}; {{Isaiah 46:4|46:4}}; {{Isaiah 48:12|48:12}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:39|Deuteronomy 32:39}}). Jesus used similar expressions for himself (see {{John 6:35|John 6:35}}; {{John 8:12|8:12}}, {{John 8:24|24}}; {{John 9:5|9:5}}; {{John 10:7|10:7}}, {{John 10:9|9}}, {{John 10:11|11}}, {{John 10:14|14}}; {{John 11:25|11:25}}; {{John 14:6|14:6}}; {{John 15:1|15:1}}, {{John 15:5|5}}).
This taunt against idol worship responded to God's raising up Cyrus. The nations hoped their idols would protect them.
*Be strong!*: The nations put their hope in things that have no strength, objects made by human craftsmen.

- The servant, representing the nation of Israel, was God's chosen one, with a purpose based on God's plans. 

- *Abraham My friend*: In Hebrew, this phrase could mean *Abraham who loves me or Abraham whom I love.* (See also {{James 2:23|James 2:23)}}.

These two prophecies about salvation for God's servant Israel ({{Isaiah 41:8-13|Isaiah 41:8–13}}, {{Isaiah 41:14-16|14–16}}) prepare for the first of the suffering servant songs (see study note on Isaiah 42:1–4).

- I have chosen you restates {{Isaiah 41:8|Isaiah 41:8}} to emphasize God's commitment and faithfulness to the people of Israel, even though they had not been faithful to him. 

- *not rejected you*: During the exile in Babylon, the people felt that God had rejected them (see {{Isaiah 49:21|Isaiah 49:21}}; {{Isaiah 54:6|54:6}}). However, God had good plans for them.

- *I am with you*: God's promise of presence (see {{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}) is central to the Bible. Because God is present, his people do not need to fear (see also {{Isaiah 43:1-2|Isaiah 43:1–2}}, {{Isaiah 43:5|5}}). 

- *I am your God*: The Lord uses covenant language to affirm that he is their God and they are his people (see also {{Jeremiah 7:23|Jeremiah 7:23}}; {{Jeremiah 31:1|31:1}}, {{Jeremiah 31:33|33}}; {{Ezekiel 14:11|Ezekiel 14:11}}; {{Ezekiel 36:28|36:28}}; {{Ezekiel 37:27|37:27}}; {{Zechariah 8:8|Zechariah 8:8}}). 

- *uphold you with My righteous right hand*: The Lord uses language similar to the exodus (compare {{Exodus 15:6|Exodus 15:6}}) to encourage Israel (see also {{Isaiah 41:13|Isaiah 41:13}}; {{Isaiah 63:12|63:12}}).

- In exile, Israel was in a lowly state. 

- God is the Redeemer. He works powerfully to rescue and restore people from sin and its consequences (for Israel, it was the exile; for an application to Jesus, see {{Luke 2:38|Luke 2:38}}; {{Luke 21:28|21:28}}; {{Romans 3:24|Romans 3:24}}; {{1 Corinthians 1:30|1 Corinthians 1:30}}; {{Galatians 4:5|Galatians 4:5}}; {{Ephesians 1:1-14|Ephesians 1:1–14}}; {{Titus 2:14|Titus 2:14}}; {{Hebrews 9:12|Hebrews 9:12}}).
When the grain is thrown into the wind, the chaff is blown away. Likewise, Israel’s enemies appeared to be strong but would easily be driven off.

*rivers … fountains … a pool of water … springs*: These pictures would have been very meaningful to people who lived by farming and raising animals. In an agrarian culture (a farming society), water meant life. Rivers, springs, and pools were signs of safety, blessing, and hope. These images also suggest that rescue from the exile in Babylon would be like a second exodus (compare {{Exodus 15:27|Exodus 15:27}}; {{Exodus 17:6|17:6}}).

This trial scene develops the Lord’s case against idolatry. Idols are nothing but a human creation, whereas God is the Creator of all things. Idols cannot speak, act, accomplish anything, or save their worshipers.

- *I have raised up on*: The God who planned the exile through Babylon also planned Israel’s return from exile through Cyrus (see {{Isaiah 41:2|Isaiah 41:2}}; see also {{Isaiah 13:17|13:17}}). 

- Although Persia is to the east, travelers to Israel and Judah had to enter from the north due to rough terrain. 

- *He will march over rulers … treads the clay*: Just as Babylon trampled Assyria, Persia would trample Babylon.
Idols and false gods could not predict the future.
The messenger with good news announced that God would come to save his people (see {{Isaiah 40:9|Isaiah 40:9}}).

- *in whom My soul delights*: God used similar words at the baptism of Jesus ({{Matthew 3:17|Matthew 3:17}}). 

- *I will put My Spirit on Him*: Any leader might be called a servant, but the Spirit's presence suggests a king from David’s line or a prophet like Moses (see {{Numbers 11:17|Numbers 11:17}}, {{Numbers 11:24-29|24–29}}). 

- Establishing justice is a king's duty (see {{Isaiah 9:6-7|Isaiah 9:6–7}}; {{Psalm 72:1|Psalm 72:1}}). 

- This king’s mission will extend beyond governing Judah to a greater mission for the nations.

The servant here is not the people of Israel (as in {{Isaiah 41:8-28|Isaiah 41:8–28}} and elsewhere in chapters {{Isaiah 41:1-48:22|41–48}}; see{{Isaiah 49:5-6|49:5–6}}). Instead, the servant is a royal figure who accomplishes his mission with care for people, especially for those who are hurting. The passage is the first of four songs about this servant ({{Isaiah 42:1-4|Isaiah 42:1–4}}; {{Isaiah 49:1-13|49:1–13}}; {{Isaiah 50:4-11|50:4–11}}; {{Isaiah 52:13-53:12|52:13–53:12}}). He brings in an era of universal justice. For the connection of the servant with Jesus Christ, see {{Matthew 12:18-21|Matthew 12:18–21}}.
*cry out or raise His voice*: The royal servant will speak with calm confidence in his message and calling from God (see also {{Isaiah 11:1-5|Isaiah 11:1–5}}).
The royal servant will be gentle with the oppressed and discouraged (see {{Isaiah 3:15|Isaiah 3:15}}; {{Isaiah 41:17|41:17}}).

*the islands*: The nations want justice and guidance on how to achieve it. The servant is like Moses, who received the law. However, the servant is greater because he brings justice to all nations, not just Israel.

- *I will keep you … to be a covenant for the people: The people* might refer to all the nations of the earth (see {{Isaiah 49:6|Isaiah 49:6}}). 

- *a light to the nations*: See also {{Isaiah 51:4|Isaiah 51:4}}; {{Acts 13:47|Acts 13:47}}.

The servant will help the spiritually blind see (see {{Isaiah 6:10|Isaiah 6:10}}; {{Isaiah 29:18|29:18}}) and free spiritual captives from sin. This is in addition to freeing those held captive during the exile in Babylon (see {{Isaiah 61:1|Isaiah 61:1}} with {{Luke 4:18|Luke 4:18}}).
*I am the LORD*: God created the world and only God can make predictions come true. God alone deserves glory and praise.

- Different geographical regions show the extremes of where people live. The entire earth is invited to praise God for his promise to save humanity. 

- Kedar and Sela were examples of desert locations ({{Isaiah 42:11|Isaiah 42:11}}; see also {{Isaiah 16:1|16:1}}; {{Isaiah 21:16-17|21:16–17}}).

- *a mighty one … a warrior*: This theme comes from God's victory at the Red Sea during the exodus ({{Exodus 15:3|Exodus 15:3}}). 

- God will defeat all his enemies to save his people ({{Isaiah 51:9|Isaiah 51:9}}; {{Isaiah 63:1-6|63:1–6}}; see also {{Psalm 54:7|Psalms 54:7}}; {{Psalm 108:9|108:9}}; {{Psalm 112:8|112:8}}).

*I have kept silent … and restrained*: Israel felt God's absence during the exile in Babylon, which happened due to their idol worship ({{Isaiah 57:11-13|Isaiah 57:11–13}}; {{2 Kings 17:6-24|2 Kings 17:6–24}}). The faithful will pray for God's presence and renewed involvement in their lives ({{Isaiah 64:12|Isaiah 64:12}}), and the Lord will answer their prayers because he is committed to their redemption ({{Isaiah 62:1|62:1}}, {{Isaiah 62:6|6}}).

The Israelites who ignored God's words and actions became spiritually blind and deaf (see {{Isaiah 6:9-10|Isaiah 6:9–10}}). They knew the truth from God's word and the prophets, but their closed minds refused to respond.
*magnify His law and make it glorious*: God’s word is a witness to his righteous rule (see {{Isaiah 1:10|Isaiah 1:10}}).

Throughout its history, Israel's sins ({{Isaiah 42:24|Isaiah 42:24}}) made it vulnerable to foreign oppressors. Many nations, especially Assyria and Babylon, became tools God used to express his anger ({{Isaiah 42:25|Isaiah 42:25}}) toward his rebellious people.
Generation after generation of Israelites did not learn their lesson, even when God disciplined them through military defeat.

- *the LORD … who created you*: The idea of creation (see study note on Isaiah 40:28) now refers to God forming the nation of Israel. 

- *He who formed you*: During the exodus, God freed his people from slavery. Similarly, God planned to bring his people back from exile to their land. Ultimately, Jesus gave his life as a ransom for all humanity ({{Matthew 20:28|Matthew 20:28}}; {{1 Timothy 2:6|1 Timothy 2:6}}; {{Hebrews 9:15|Hebrews 9:15}}).

- *I have called you by your name; you are Mine!*: Despite having faced his wrath, the people of Israel are still God’s chosen people.
In this promise of salvation, the Lord spoke directly to his people.

- Conquering forces are compared to flooding rivers (see {{Isaiah 8:8|Isaiah 8:8}}). 

- *I will be with you*: God promises to stay with his people to protect and care for them (see {{Isaiah 7:14|Isaiah 7:14}}; {{Isaiah 41:10|41:10}}; {{Isaiah 43:5|43:5}}; {{Isaiah 45:14|45:14}}). 

- Israel faced God's judgment as the fire of oppression during the exile in Babylon.
One of God’s purposes in restoring his people was to display his glory to the watching world.

The Lord here called on Israel, his blind servant, to be his star witness in a mock trial against idols and false gods. Israel knew that the Lord alone is God, and the people had experienced his salvation.

*You are My witnesses*: By their very presence in exile, Israel was evidence that God is truly God. He predicted the exile long beforehand, and now it had come to pass. God alone is the true God because he speaks and acts and controls all of history. Idols and false gods could do none of these things. Israel would later become even greater evidence because God had also predicted their redemption ({{Isaiah 43:11-12|Isaiah 43:11–12}}).
The Lord promised Israel that it would be freed from Babylon. This redemption would be similar to Israel's past freedom from Egypt but even greater in some ways ({{Isaiah 43:18|Isaiah 43:18}}).
God wanted the Israelites to remember the exodus from Egypt. However, they needed to focus on the amazing event that was about to happen, instead of staying stuck in the past.
One purpose of redemption is to honor God through the praises of the redeemed (see {{1 Peter 2:9|1 Peter 2:9}}).

Israel's history of rebellion led them into many crises. Their rebellion was so strong that they refused to ask God for help. When they did pray, their wickedness often caused God not to hear their prayers ({{Isaiah 1:15|Isaiah 1:15}}).

God alone can blot out sins. This means he completely removes and forgives them.

It does not matter how many sins a person has committed or how serious they are. God has the power to forgive them all (see also {{Isaiah 44:22|Isaiah 44:22}}).
*spokesmen*: God held the kings of Israel and Judah especially responsible for leading the nation into sin (see {{2 Kings 21:1-26|2 Kings 21}}).

The promise of salvation gave Israel a future. Even though the people had sinned, God would still use them to bless the next generation ({{Isaiah 44:3|Isaiah 44:3}}). 

The past had been dark because of their sin (see {{Isaiah 43:22-28|Isaiah 43:22–28}}). But the future would be different. God would begin a new time of blessing. His Spirit would change the people and make this new beginning possible.

- The restoration theme is connected with God’s promise to pour out the Spirit (see also {{Isaiah 32:15-17|Isaiah 32:15–17}}; {{Joel 2:28-32|Joel 2:28–32}}; {{Acts 2:16-18|Acts 2:16–18}}). 

- *on your descendants … your offspring*: The next generation of Israelites offered hope.
This passage uses the form of a trial speech to press God’s argument that disgrace comes to all who trust in idols and false gods.

*He takes some of it to warm himself … He also fashions it into a god and worships it*: This description of making an idol is full of sarcasm and mocks the foolishness of idol worshipers (see also {{Isaiah 44:19|Isaiah 44:19}}).
*closed their minds*: Idol worshipers do not see the irony in using one part of a log for warmth and another part as their god.
The Lord promised to forgive the sins of Israel.
All creation is called to celebrate God’s redemption of Israel (compare {{Isaiah 1:2|Isaiah 1:2}}).
The Lord alone is sovereign over history. He raised up Cyrus of Persia to execute judgment on Babylon and restore Israel to the Holy Land.

False prophets and diviners used forbidden methods to predict the future. Eventually, God would reveal them as liars who believed something that is not true (see {{Isaiah 3:2|Isaiah 3:2}}; {{Isaiah 9:15|9:15}}; {{Isaiah 47:13|47:13}}; {{Deuteronomy 18:10-11|Deuteronomy 18:10–11}}).

The sudden loss of natural resources sometimes shows divine judgment (see {{Isaiah 42:15|Isaiah 42:15}}; compare {{Isaiah 43:20|43:20}}). Here, however, God's ability to dry up streams with only a word shows his power to fulfill his promises through Cyrus of Persia.

*My shepherd*: Cyrus did more than just allow the Jews to return home. He led a major project to rebuild Jerusalem and restore the temple (see {{Isaiah 45:13|Isaiah 45:13}}; {{Ezra 1:2-4|Ezra 1:2–4}}; {{Ezra 6:3-5|6:3–5}}).

- *His anointed*: This title, usually for David or the Messiah, is used here for Cyrus. Cyrus was anointed because he was chosen for a special mission. No other foreign ruler received this title (compare {{1 Samuel 10:1|1 Samuel 10:1}}; {{Romans 13:1|Romans 13:1}}). 

- *whose right hand I have grasped*: The Lord would help Cyrus defeat Babylon (see {{Isaiah 43:14|Isaiah 43:14}}).
*so that you may know*: Cyrus's victories show that the Lord can fulfill his plans. Idols and false gods cannot do this (see {{Isaiah 41:21-29|Isaiah 41:21–29}}).

*I call you by name*: Cyrus did not know the Lord, but the Lord knew him. Isaiah predicted the rescuer Cyrus by name 150 years before he was born. This prophecy would show the exiles that the Lord is truly God and that he knows the future.
*light … darkness … prosperity … calamity*: Everything is under God’s control.
*pot … the potter … him … his father*: It is foolish for a creature to question the wisdom of its creator.

The Lord addresses those who doubt his decision to use a non-believing king for his plans. As the Creator, he is free and has complete authority. He promised to return his people to their land and would use anyone he chooses to fulfill that promise.
*Egypt … Cush … Sabeans*: Israel's restoration would give them new sovereignty. Foreign nations would honor God. Recognizing God's blessing on His people, they would also honor them.
Israel will never again face humiliation, disgrace, oppression, harassment, or abuse. These declarations suggest this promise will be fulfilled at the end of time.
Ancient pagan people saw the world as a place of empty chaos. However, God's plans are good. He created the world from the start to live in harmony with him.

Salvation comes only from the Lord. He is the creator, the revealer, and the one who carries out his will in human history. He promised to start a new era of salvation and righteousness (see {{Isaiah 45:8|Isaiah 45:8}}). Every person will submit to God, either by choice or not ({{Isaiah 45:23-24|Isaiah 45:23–24}}).

- *Turn to Me … all the ends of the earth*: All people need to seek the Lord, the true God who created everything, while he is available ({{Isaiah 55:6|Isaiah 55:6}}). 

- In God there is salvation, the only hope for all people ({{Isaiah 45:8|Isaiah 45:8}}).

- God's words are always true. When God swears by his own name, it shows he will never break his promise (see also {{Isaiah 14:24|Isaiah 14:24}}; {{Isaiah 54:9|54:9}}; {{Isaiah 62:8|62:8}}; {{Hebrews 6:13|Hebrews 6:13}}). 

- *Every knee … every tongue*: At the end of time, all nations will accept his authority, either willingly or unwillingly (see {{Romans 14:11|Romans 14:11}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:25-27|1 Corinthians 15:25–27}}; {{Philippians 2:10-11|Philippians 2:10–11}}).
In this context, the people include everyone who seeks salvation from the Lord, even those from other nations ({{Isaiah 45:22|Isaiah 45:22}}).

- *Marduk-bel* was the most important god in the Babylonian group of gods. *Bel*, similar to *Baal*, meant lordship. 

- Nebo (*Nabu, Nebu*), the patron god of Babylonian scribes, was believed to be the son of Marduk-bel. 

- Instead of being celebrated at a Babylonian festival, people would transport these gods on ox carts and discard them, as the Babylonian people rejected them.

This taunt was against the self-contradiction of Babylonian religion.

A taunt is a mocking song or speech. In this passage, the prophet makes fun of Babylon’s beliefs. The message shows that their religion does not make sense.

- *the remnant of the house of Israel*: This refers to the survivors after Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BC. 

- The Lord, the Creator of humanity, cares for and carries his people, unlike the Babylonian idols that need carrying. 

- *sustained from the womb, carried along since birth*: The Lord chose Israel even before it became a nation (see also {{Isaiah 49:5|Isaiah 49:5}}).
Many exiles felt hopeless and doubted God's promise to rescue them. God addressed this doubt.

God knows the future before it happens; he controls all events, and his actions match his words ({{Isaiah 41:4|Isaiah 41:4}}, {{Isaiah 41:26|26}}). He is the first and the last ({{Isaiah 44:6|Isaiah 44:6}}; {{Isaiah 48:12|48:12}}).
The swift bird of prey from the east refers to Cyrus, the Persian king (see study note on Isaiah 41:2).
Formerly, Israel cared little for doing right (literally *righteousness;* see also {{Isaiah 58:2|Isaiah 58:2}}; {{Isaiah 59:9|59:9}}).

- The good news for Israel was that God was coming to make things right (literally *I will bring my righteousness near;* see {{Isaiah 40:9|Isaiah 40:9}}; {{Isaiah 51:5|51:5}}). 

- *adorn Israel with My splendor*: Unlike a craftsman who gives material splendor to an idol ({{Isaiah 44:13|Isaiah 44:13}}), the Lord gives true dignity to his people.
To sit in the dust was a way of expressing humiliation.

In this taunt against Babylon, the nation is described as a proud queen.

But she is brought low and humiliated. Instead of ruling, she is forced to work like a servant girl.
God will bring justice to the world by punishing those who oppose him and oppress his people (see {{Isaiah 34:8|Isaiah 34:8}}). This will remove wickedness.

Babylon was known for its confidence and arrogance (see {{Isaiah 14:13-17|Isaiah 14:13–17}}; {{Daniel 4:30|Daniel 4:30}}). The nation's charms, magic, and wisdom could not stop the disaster planned for it.
The people of Israel had provoked God’s wrath, prompting him to use Babylon to punish them. Now wicked Babylon itself would be punished.

- *I am, and there is none besides me*: This was a claim to divinity (compare {{Isaiah 45:5|Isaiah 45:5}}; {{Isaiah 47:10|47:10}}). Only the Lord can make such a claim. It is extremely arrogant for any created thing, including a nation, to say this. 

- Being a widow or losing one's children was considered a disgrace.
People often used witchcraft and magic to protect themselves from evil and ensure a happy future.

Here, *wisdom* and *knowledge* likely refer sarcastically to the false knowledge from occult practices. This false knowledge led Babylon away from the truth and into disaster ({{Isaiah 47:11|Isaiah 47:11}}).
When disaster struck, Babylon turned to occult practices for help, but found none.
Babylon was advanced in astronomy, which the astrologers and stargazers used as a form of divination (see {{Daniel 2:2|Daniel 2:2}}, {{Daniel 2:10|10}}; {{Daniel 5:7|5:7}}).
*Jacob … Judah*: Isaiah usually focused on Judah, but here he spoke to all the tribes of Israel.
Israel was religious but not truly committed to the Lord.
This prophecy is a *disputation,* a speech in which the prophet argues a set of points against his audience.
The Lord urges Israel to abandon its long history of rebellion and pay attention to his words. In Hebrew, the word for *listening* often means the same as *obeying* or acting on what is heard.
The Lord had warned Israel about what was going to happen in the exile.
Although Israel often did not believe God's past predictions, God revealed new things they had not heard. Specifically, God revealed that Babylon would fall and Israel would be restored.
The exile in Babylon was a period of intense suffering (compare {{Deuteronomy 4:20|Deuteronomy 4:20}}) that God used to purify Israel.

*For My own sake … I will act*: Israel's exile made other nations question the Lord's character and reputation. These nations did not see that Israel's wickedness caused the exile. Instead, they saw it as a failure of Israel's God to protect his people and their land (see {{Isaiah 36:19-20|Isaiah 36:19–20}}; {{Isaiah 37:12|37:12}}; {{Ezekiel 36:19-26|Ezekiel 36:19–26}}).
This final trial speech reviews the arguments of {{Isaiah 40:1-48:22|Isaiah 40–48}} and presents the final conclusion.
*I have brought him, and he will succeed in his mission*: Cyrus would humiliate Babylon and liberate Israel ({{Isaiah 45:1-4|Isaiah 45:1–4}}).

- *I have not spoken in secret*: God's promises are clear, though they do not always specify how or when they will happen. 

- *And now the Lord GOD has sent me, accompanied by His Spirit*: The identity of the one sent is unclear. Isaiah might be referring to himself as a prophet inspired by the Spirit, speaking God's words to Israel. The connection with the spirit suggests it refers to the promised servant, the Messiah. 

- The presence of the Spirit ensures the servant's success.

- Peace and righteousness will be established when the kingdom of God fully comes (see {{Isaiah 66:12|Isaiah 66:12}}). 

- *like a river … like waves of the sea*: There will be abundant peace and overflowing righteousness (compare {{Amos 5:24|Amos 5:24}}). Israel could have had this if its people had listened to God.

*Your descendants … as the sand*: This fulfills God's promise to Abraham (see {{Genesis 22:17|Genesis 22:17}}). In contrast, the Israelites were almost destroyed during the exile in Babylon (see {{Isaiah 44:26|Isaiah 44:26}}).

*not thirst … rock … water gushed out*: These reminders of God’s provision in the exodus provide a fitting summary of what he would do to rescue Israel from captivity in Babylon (see {{Numbers 20:11|Numbers 20:11}}).

This phrase, *There is not peace … for the wicked* (also {{Isaiah 57:21|Isaiah 57:21}}), highlights the clear difference between the godly and the wicked (see {{Isaiah 66:24|66:24}}). Peace represents God's kingdom, which does not include the wicked.

- *O distant peoples*: The servant's work would not be limited to Israel. His ministry would reach people in faraway nations (see {{Isaiah 42:4|Isaiah 42:4}}, {{Isaiah 42:10|10}}, {{Isaiah 42:12|12}}; {{Isaiah 51:5|51:5}}; {{Isaiah 60:9|60:9}}; {{Isaiah 66:19|66:19}}). 

- *called Me from the womb … He named Me*: The promised servant's prophetic call was like Jeremiah's call (see {{Jeremiah 1:5|Jeremiah 1:5}}; see also {{Galatians 1:15|Galatians 1:15}}). It was not a general call but a very specific, personal one (see also {{Isaiah 43:1|Isaiah 43:1}}; {{Isaiah 45:3-4|45:3–4}}).

This is traditionally seen as the second of four songs about a suffering servant (see study note on Isaiah 42:1–4). The servant's role in suffering becomes clearer (see also {{Isaiah 50:4-9|Isaiah 50:4–9}}; {{Isaiah 52:13-53:12|52:13–53:12}}).

The messages of Isaiah 49:1–6; 50:4–9 and 52:13 – 53:12 talked more about God’s servant. It isn’t known for sure who this servant was at the time of these prophecies. It may have been the prophet Isaiah. It may have been someone who helped God’s people while they were in exile. God set the servant apart to do God’s work.

That work was to bring Jacob’s family line back to God. This meant that the servant would help God’s people live the way God wanted them to. They would truly live as God’s people and be faithful to him. It also meant that the servant would help them return from exile to their land.

The servant’s work was also to be a light for the Gentiles. This way everyone on earth would know God. Everyone would trust God to be their Saviour.

The servant didn’t do his work by using violence. He was gentle and spoke the words God taught him. His words were like a sword. He was treated badly. He suffered and was put to death because of the sins of God’s people. He was willing for this to happen even though he hadn’t done anything wrong.

In this way he became a sin offering for God’s people. Suffering in this way is different from the pattern that Job’s friends had noticed. They had noticed that people who did foolish and sinful things were made to suffer. God’s servant was suffering even though he hadn’t done sinful and foolish things. He was suffering in order to help God’s people.

God’s servant showed that suffering for others can lead to their salvation. This helped Jesus’s followers understand the work that Jesus did when he died on the cross. Many New Testament writers used words from these chapters about God’s servant to describe Jesus.

God planned to rescue the Israelites from exile. But an important question remained. How could sinful Israel serve the Holy One again?

God would make a way to remove Israel’s sin. He would restore their fellowship with him. This means he would bring them back into a right relationship with himself.

The way would be through the promised Servant. This Servant would come for Israel and for all nations. He was first introduced in {{Isaiah 42:1-9|Isaiah 42:1–9}}. n this passage, he becomes the main focus.

*My mouth*: The servant's mission would be prophetic (see {{Isaiah 11:4|Isaiah 11:4}}; {{Ephesians 6:17|Ephesians 6:17}}; {{Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12}}; {{Revelation 1:16|Revelation 1:16}}; {{Revelation 2:12|2:12}}, {{Revelation 2:16|16}}; {{Revelation 19:15|19:15}}).

The suffering servant would emerge from Israel (see {{Isaiah 41:8|Isaiah 41:8}}) and would be the true Israel. He would serve as both king ({{Isaiah 42:1|Isaiah 42:1}}) and prophet ({{Isaiah 49:1|Isaiah 49:1}}). He would be anointed with the Spirit of God ({{Isaiah 61:1|Isaiah 61:1}}). God would appoint him ({{Isaiah 48:16|Isaiah 48:16}}) as a faithful witness to God's plans ({{Isaiah 43:12|43:12}}; {{Isaiah 48:20|48:20}}).

In his mission to both Israel and other nations ({{Isaiah 49:6|Isaiah 49:6}}), the suffering servant would face rejection and disgrace while remaining faithful, unlike the nation of Israel (see {{Isaiah 50:4-9|Isaiah 50:4–9}}). His suffering would be for the sake of God's chosen people. 

Jesus became the ultimate fulfillment of the suffering servant (see study note on Isaiah 52:13–53:12).

- *I have labored in vain*: Even though people stubbornly refuse his message, the servant will still reach out to them. 

- *My vindication is with the LORD*: Despite discouragement and suffering, the servant will continue to perform his duty faithfully, trusting God for the outcome. God promised to reward the servant’s faithfulness (see also {{Isaiah 40:10|Isaiah 40:10}}; {{Isaiah 50:8|50:8}}).

*a light for the nations*: As the Messiah (God's chosen one), the servant's mission would reach the entire world (see {{Isaiah 11:10|Isaiah 11:10}}, {{Isaiah 11:12|12}}; {{Isaiah 42:6|42:6}}). The apostle Paul explained his mission to the Gentiles based on this prophecy ({{Acts 13:47|Acts 13:47}}; {{Acts 26:23|26:23}}).

- The promised servant will be disliked and rejected by the nations (see {{Isaiah 52:14-53:5|Isaiah 52:14–53:5}}) and by his own people (see also {{Isaiah 50:6-7|50:6–7}}; {{Isaiah 53:8-9|53:8–9}}). 

- Kings and princes will bow low to show respect and humility to the servant (see also {{Isaiah 52:15|Isaiah 52:15}}). God will lift him up after he suffers. God is loyal to his servant.

God acts at the right time to achieve his goals ({{Acts 1:7|Acts 1:7}}; {{2 Corinthians 6:2|2 Corinthians 6:2}}). Israel returned to rebuild the land of Israel after the exile in Babylon. The land was restored, and the city was rebuilt, starting with Cyrus’s decree ({{Isaiah 44:26-28|Isaiah 44:26–28}}).

- Like a shepherd, the Lord in his mercy will guide the returning exiles beside cool waters. He promised to comfort them and meet their needs (see also {{Isaiah 40:11|Isaiah 40:11}}; {{Psalm 23:1|Psalm 23:1}}). 

- *roads … highways*: The Lord would open up the way of salvation.
The remnant would come from the north (that is, Babylon and Persia), from the west by sea, and from as far south as Egypt.
This hymn of praise is in response to the salvation that the servant would make possible.

The prophet gave reasons to rejoice ({{Isaiah 49:8-13|Isaiah 49:8–13}}), but the exiles still thought about the disaster. Babylon invaded, destroyed Jerusalem, and took the people of Judah into exile. There, they felt abandoned and forgotten.
*as jewelry and put them on like a bride*: Just as a wedding is festive and public, God's restoration of Israel would be visible to everyone (see also {{Isaiah 61:10|Isaiah 61:10}}).

- The population growth would extend beyond Israel to include people from other nations who turn to the Lord (see {{Isaiah 56:6-8|Isaiah 56:6–8}}; {{Revelation 7:9|Revelation 7:9}}). 

- *make room*: The increased population would need space far beyond Israel's traditional borders (see also {{Zechariah 2:4|Zechariah 2:4}}).

*bring your sons … carry your daughters*: The powerful rulers of the nations, some of whom had once harmed children in Israel, would help them return to Zion (see also {{Isaiah 60:3-9|Isaiah 60:3–9}}). In other parts of Isaiah, he imagined people from foreign nations coming to Zion to worship the Lord (see {{Isaiah 2:2-4|Isaiah 2:2–4}}).

- *you will know that I am the LORD*: The surprising role reversal, with kings and queens serving the humble exiles upon their return, will show God's power to do the unimaginable (see also {{Isaiah 60:16|Isaiah 60:16}}). 

- The godly will face temporary disgrace during the exile in Babylon but would not ultimately be put to shame, as the idolaters and ungodly were.
*be snatched … be delivered*: The people considered it nearly impossible that they would be rescued from their oppressors.
The Lord is like a warrior who fights to protect his children, as promised to Abraham ({{Genesis 12:3|Genesis 12:3}}; see also {{Isaiah 54:15|Isaiah 54:15}}).

- God was not responsible for the people's problems; their sin caused their exile (see also {{Isaiah 59:1-15|Isaiah 59:1–15}}). 

- Jerusalem, the main city of Judah ({{Psalm 87:5-6|Psalm 87:5–6}}), was destroyed, and the people of Judah went into exile in 586 BC.
This argument shows that God was not forced to abandon Israel. Therefore, he could choose to accept the nation back as his people if he wished.

- *Why did no one answer*: The people did not respond to God's repeated call to trust him and repent of their sins. They were deaf and stubborn (see {{Isaiah 6:9-10|Isaiah 6:9–10}}; {{Isaiah 29:18|29:18}}; {{Isaiah 35:5|35:5}}; {{Isaiah 42:18-19|42:18–19}}). 

- The Lord came and called the people through the prophets (see also {{Isaiah 65:1-3|Isaiah 65:1–3}}).

- *do I lack the strength to deliver you?*: God could rescue Israel and Judah from the Assyrians and Babylonians, but he first had to address his people's sinfulness (see {{Isaiah 59:1|Isaiah 59:1}}). 

- *My rebuke dries up the sea*: This refers to the parting of the Red Sea during the exodus from Egypt ({{Exodus 14:21-22|Exodus 14:21–22}}).

People connected events like darkness and wearing mourning clothes with the day of the Lord ({{Isaiah 13:10|Isaiah 13:10}}; see study note on Isaiah 2:5–22). The mention of darkness might refer to the plague of darkness in Egypt ({{Exodus 10:21|Exodus 10:21}}).
The Lord, who never gets tired ({{Isaiah 40:28|Isaiah 40:28}}), sends the servant with good news (see {{Isaiah 40:28-31|40:28–31}}) to comfort those who are tired (see study note on Isaiah 40:1–31).
This is the third of four servant songs (see study note on Isaiah 42:1–4). The loyal and suffering servant represents an ideal Israel. This image came true in Jesus Christ.

*struck Me … tore out My beard … scorn and spittle*: These connections with the experience of Jesus at his crucifixion are too close to not be intentional. Jesus is the true suffering servant (see {{Matthew 27:27-31|Matthew 27:27–31}}).

- Externally, the servant would be disgraced and shamed by others. However, inside himself he would wait calmly for God to prove that he was right (see {{Isaiah 29:22|Isaiah 29:22}}; {{Isaiah 54:4|54:4}}; {{Isaiah 61:7|61:7}}). He trusted that God would defend him and clear his name.

- *set My face like flint*: The servant would be determined to follow God's will (see {{Luke 9:51|Luke 9:51}}).

- *The One who vindicates Me is near*: God defends those who suffer for following his will. Vindication is an act of God where he lifts up those wrongly shamed and punishes the wicked, proud, and arrogant (see also {{2 Thessalonians 1:6-9|2 Thessalonians 1:6–9}}). 

- *confront … a case against Me*: Trust in God’s vindication removes fear and strengthens faith (see {{Romans 8:31-34|Romans 8:31–34}}).

*Who is there to condemn Me?*: This question expects the answer, “No one!” The servant is confident that no one can prove him guilty.

This statement points forward to the New Testament teaching about justification (God declaring a person to be right with him). Paul speaks about this in {{Romans 8:31-35|Romans 8:31–35}}).

- To see if someone respects the Lord, observe how they treat God's righteous servant. This idea is similar to the statement Jesus made that no one can reach the Father except through him ({{John 14:6|John 14:6}}). 

- Those who trust in the Lord have strong hope for the future (see {{Isaiah 12:2|Isaiah 12:2}}).
This is a call for response to the servant’s ministry.

*all you who kindle a fire*: Spiritually complacent people do not respond to God. They may feel comfortable and secure now, but they will soon experience great suffering (see {{Isaiah 66:24|Isaiah 66:24}}).
The rock and the quarry represent Abraham and Sarah ({{Isaiah 51:2|Isaiah 51:2}}).
This prophecy urges trust in the Lord. Each of its three parts starts with the phrase *Listen to Me* ({{Isaiah 51:1|Isaiah 51:1}}, {{Isaiah 51:4|4}}, {{Isaiah 51:7|7}}).
*Abraham … I blessed him and multiplied him*: The exiled community had decreased in number. They needed to have faith that God could restore them again to a healthy and thriving population.
*Eden … the garden of the LORD*: God’s salvation will one day reestablish conditions like those in which human beings first lived (see {{Genesis 2:1-3:24|Genesis 2–3}}).

- *a law … My justice*: The servant's work will succeed because justice will guide God's kingdom on earth (see {{Isaiah 42:1-4|Isaiah 42:1–4}}). 

- *a light to the nations*: The nations will accept the Lord and his revelation (see also {{Isaiah 42:6|Isaiah 42:6}}; {{Isaiah 49:6|49:6}}; {{Isaiah 60:1-3|60:1–3}}; {{Isaiah 66:19-23|66:19–23}}; {{Matthew 4:15-16|Matthew 4:15–16}}; {{Luke 2:32|Luke 2:32}}; {{John 1:4-9|John 1:4–9}}; {{John 12:35-50|12:35–50}}; {{Acts 13:47|Acts 13:47}}).
God is strong enough to crush his enemies and rescue his people, such as when he rescued Israel in the exodus (see {{Isaiah 51:9|Isaiah 51:9}}; {{Exodus 6:6|Exodus 6:6}}; {{Exodus 15:16|15:16}}).
*die like gnats*: Many wicked people will die on the day of God's judgment.

- *My law in your hearts*: The Lord wants his people to understand, value, and follow his word (see also {{Psalm 37:31|Psalm 37:31}}; {{Jeremiah 31:33|Jeremiah 31:33}}). 

- Those who follow the Lord often face ridicule and insults (see also {{Matthew 5:10-12|Matthew 5:10–12}}).

- *Awake, awake*: God does not sleep. This prayer asks God to act immediately to save his people (see {{Isaiah 52:1|Isaiah 52:1}}; see especially God’s military clothing in {{Isaiah 59:17|59:17}}). 

- *in generations of old*: The exodus from Egypt was an act of redemption. It showed God’s power as he made a path of escape ({{Isaiah 51:10|Isaiah 51:10}}) for his people (see also {{Isaiah 11:15|11:15}}).

- *you have forgotten the LORD*: The Lord will never forget Israel (see {{Isaiah 44:21|Isaiah 44:21}}; {{Isaiah 49:15|49:15}}), so they should remember him. 

- The Creator of the world also created the nation of Israel.
The exile in Babylon brought harsh conditions like imprisonment, starvation, and death.
*I am the LORD*: The Lord uses this phrase to show he is the covenant God. It assures his people that his words are true and his actions are reliable (see {{Isaiah 27:3-4|Isaiah 27:3–4}}).

- *My words in your mouth*: The focus shifted back to the servant.

- *You are My people*: Israel was the covenant community.

- *Awake, awake!*: Israel used these words in a prayer to the Lord ({{Isaiah 51:9|Isaiah 51:9}}). Israel's problems were not because God was slow to act. Instead, the people were slow to believe God's promises. 

- *the cup of His fury*: The Lord will give judgment in a just and measured way. He will judge in the right amount and at the right time.

Those who come under his judgment are described as drinking from a cup of his wrath. This is a picture that shows they must fully experience the results of their sin (see also {{Matthew 26:39|Matthew 26:39}}).
The prophet called the people of Israel to be done with their past and to anticipate God’s future for them.

*Your sons have fainted*: This phrase shows how terrible Jerusalem’s destruction was. Even children became weak and collapsed from hunger and suffering.

The book of Lamentations also describes this deep sorrow and pain ({{Lamentations 1:13|Lamentations 1:13}}, {{Lamentations 1:22|22}}; {{Lamentations 2:11-12|2:11–12}}, {{Lamentations 2:19|19}}).
God will defend Israel, just as he did when Assyria attacked Jerusalem ({{Isaiah 38:6|Isaiah 38:6}}).
The Babylonians were the ones who caused destruction, war, and famine ({{Isaiah 51:19|Isaiah 51:19}}).

- This second call to wake up (see {{Isaiah 51:17|Isaiah 51:17}}) was in preparation for a glorious future. 

- *holy city*: The new city would be holy because its citizens would be holy (see {{Isaiah 4:3|Israel 4:3}}). 

- *will no longer enter you*: Things that are unclean will not be permitted to enter the holy city (see {{Revelation 21:27|Revelation 21:27}}).
*You were sold for nothing … you will be redeemed*: The Lord was in control when he allowed his people to be captured by their enemies. He stayed in control and could save them if he wanted to.
*went down to Egypt to live, then Assyria oppressed them*: The exodus from exile would resemble Israel's past exodus from Egypt.

- The oppressors would shout with joy because they thought they had defeated both Israel and its God. 

- *My name is blasphemed continually all day long*: The state of God's people influences God's reputation in the eyes of the world (see {{Isaiah 37:6|Isaiah 37:6}}, {{Isaiah 37:23|23}}; {{Isaiah 48:11|48:11}}).
Just as God revealed himself to Moses before the exodus ({{Exodus 3:15|Exodus 3:15}}), he will reveal himself in the future rescue from exile.

- *How beautiful on the mountains*: See {{Nahum 1:15|Nahum 1:15}}; {{Romans 10:15|Romans 10:15}}. 

- The good news is more than ending the exile in Babylon. It also points to the peace and salvation of the age to come ({{Isaiah 54:13-14|Isaiah 54:13–14}}; see {{Isaiah 40:9-10|40:9–10}}; {{Isaiah 41:27|41:27}}).

This passage uses poetry to describe God’s promise to save his people. Their sin had separated them from God (it had broken their relationship with him). God promised to remove that separation and bring them back to himself.

The picture is of a city surrounded by enemy armies. The people inside the city are waiting for news. They hope to hear that their hero has defeated the enemy and won the battle.

Paul uses these words to speak about the good news of the Lord Jesus Christ ({{Romans 10:15|Romans 10:15}}). He shows that this promise is fulfilled in the message about Jesus.

- The watchmen were those seeking news of Zion's redemption. 

- *the LORD returns to Zion*: The sin of those who lived in the city had driven God away.
*the salvation of our God*: God saving his people from shame hints at a greater victory. God will rule triumphantly everywhere (note the similarities with {{Psalm 98:1-3|Psalm 98:1–3}}).
Here the imagery of leaving the unclean enemy city encourages the people to purify themselves by turning away from all known sin. Those who carry home the sacred objects of the Lord need to be pure.

This is a call to escape the captivity of sin (see {{Isaiah 48:20|Isaiah 48:20}} on leaving physical captivity in Babylon). See also {{2 Corinthians 6:17|2 Corinthians 6:17}}; {{2 Timothy 2:19|2 Timothy 2:19}}.

- *you will not leave in a hurry*: At the time of the exodus, the people had to leave quickly (see {{Exodus 12:11|Exodus 12:11}}, {{Exodus 12:31-36|31–36}}). Isaiah highlighted this difference to emphasize the newness of God's plan. 

- *your rear guard*: See {{Exodus 13:21|Exodus 13:21}}; {{Exodus 14:19-20|14:19–20}}.
*prosper … highly exalted*: The servant will be wise and successful, standing with the great and noble. Similar terms describe God in {{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}} and {{Isaiah 57:15|57:15}}.

This is the fourth of four passages that speak about the promised servant (see study note on Isaiah 42:1–4). The Hebrew poem is carefully constructed in five three-line stanzas.It begins with the servant’s exaltation ({{Isaiah 52:13|52:13}}), proceeds to his humiliation ({{Isaiah 52:14-53:9|52:14–53:9}}), and ends with his exaltation ({{Isaiah 53:10-12|53:10–12}}). 

The faithful servant’s suffering would bring reconciliation between God and humans. The Lord Jesus perfectly fulfilled this prophecy (see {{Isaiah 40:1-31|Isaiah 40}}; {{Matthew 8:17|Matthew 8:17}}; {{Acts 8:30-35|Acts 8:30–35}}; {{Romans 10:15-17|Romans 10:15–17}}; {{Romans 15:21|15:21}}; {{1 Peter 2:24-25|1 Peter 2:24–25}}).
*many were appalled*: No one expected that the rescuer would suffer and die.
Despite the servant’s greatness, the actual way he would appear on earth would surprise people.

- *sprinkle many nation*: They will be amazed that a rescuer appears weak and helpless, leaving them speechless. 

- What they will see and what they will understand will be in complete contrast to anything they had previously imagined.

- *our message*: Scholars have debated who the speaker could be. The main possibilities are: 

- a faithful remnant of Israel, and

- Isaiah himself.

Most likely, Isaiah the prophet was speaking for and with Israel.

- *the arm*: This refers to God's strength, vividly described in the previous chapters (see {{Isaiah 50:2|Isaiah 50:2}}; {{Isaiah 51:5|51:5}}, {{Isaiah 51:9|9}}; {{Isaiah 52:10|52:10}}). It would show itself in weakness and apparent helplessness through the servant's humiliation and exaltation (see {{1 Corinthians 1:27-30|1 Corinthians 1:27–30}}).

- *a tender shoot … out of dry ground*: Such a plant is at risk of dying out (compare {{Isaiah 37:27|Isaiah 37:27}}). It struggles to survive, much less offer anything to others. 

- *no stately form or majesty*: The servant seemed to lack greatness or obvious royal splendor (see {{Isaiah 52:13-15|Isaiah 52:13–15}}). 

- *to attract us*: People prefer leaders who are good-looking and charismatic. The servant would be neither.

- *a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief*: The servant would suffer deeply. He would know pain and sadness from personal experience.

He would fully experience the results of human sin and the fall (the time when the first humans disobeyed God and brought suffering into the world).

- *we esteemed Him not*: People would not see how someone weak and insignificant could help them, so they would ignore his suffering.

- The uncaring world might think the servant caused his own suffering, not realizing he suffered for them. 

- *infirmities … sorrows*: These descriptions of the servant's humiliation contrast with those of his exaltation.

- *He was pierced*: See also {{Zechariah 12:10|Zechariah 12:10}}. 

- *crushed … punishment … stripes*: These were typical punishments for crimes. Sin is a crime against God. 

- *brought us peace*: The Hebrew word *shalom* is usually translated as "peace." *Shalom* means experiencing wholeness in body, mind, and relationships with others. The servant would be injured so humanity can be whole and healthy in all aspects of life (see also {{Isaiah 57:18|Isaiah 57:18}}). We do not need to suffer divine punishment for our sins because the servant has already done so (see {{Galatians 1:4|Galatians 1:4}}).
*gone astray … turned to his own way*: These phrases are metaphors for sin (see also {{Romans 3:10-18|Romans 3:10–18}}).
See {{1 Peter 2:21-25|1 Peter 2:21–25}} to see how Jesus Christ fulfills this prophecy.
The Ethiopian eunuch was reading this passage when Philip met him (see {{Acts 8:32-33|Acts 8:32–33}}).

- *By oppression and judgment*: The servant will not receive legal protection or a proper defense. 

- *cut off from the land of the living*: To die in midlife was understood to be God’s judgment.

- *no violence, nor was any deceit*: See {{1 Peter 2:21-25|1 Peter 2:21–25}}.

- *with a rich man in His death* (see {{Matthew 27:57-61|Matthew 27:57–61}}): Although the Bible often views riches as a blessing from God, it frequently condemns the rich as dishonest and oppressive. The point here might be ironic: This good man would be buried with oppressors.

- The servant's grief would lead to a greater good: the forgiveness and reconciliation of sinful humanity. Note also God’s good plan to prosper and exalt the servant.

- *when His soul is made a guilt offering*: The servant's suffering served as a substitute for others, similar to animal sacrifices in the Temple. 

- Having many descendants and enjoying a long life are rewards for living wisely and righteously (see {{Proverbs 3:2|Proverbs 3:2}}; {{Proverbs 17:6|17:6}}; {{Proverbs 20:7|20:7}}). Because the servant trusted his fate to God, he would receive eternal rewards from God, who vindicates the righteous (see {{Philippians 2:9-11|Philippians 2:9–11}}).
The final stanza of the poem first explains why the servant suffered and was treated unjustly in the place of others; it then explains what the result of that obedience would be.

- H*is knowledge*: This does not mean knowledge in the sense of ideas in the mind. It refers to everything the servant would live through. It includes his obedience, his suffering, and his close relationship with God.

- Because the servant obeys God fully, many people can be put right with God. This is called justification (God declaring a person to be right with him). He can do this because he will carry and bear their sins (see {{Genesis 15:6|Genesis 15:6}}; {{Romans 5:18-19|Romans 5:18–19}}).

- *a portion*: See {{Philippians 2:9-11|Philippians 2:9–11}}. 

- *He was numbered with the transgressors: Transgressors* (Hebrew *poshe‘im*) is a stronger word than *sinners* and is important in Isaiah. It refers to those who defy lawful authority, in this case, God. 

- *intercession for the transgressors*: The servant would pray for sinners while suffering (see {{Exodus 32:30|Exodus 32:30}}; {{Luke 23:34|Luke 23:34}}).
